solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Closely follow The Three Blind Mice scandal?

definitions.meaning: to drive right behind another vehicle, too near its rear
the farmer's wife cut off the mice's tails; a scandal is named with the suffix -gate, after Watergate

explanation.surface: A puzzling line about following someone closely and a nursery-rhyme scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: Scandals get named '-gate' after Watergate, and the nursery rhyme's mice lose their tails to a carving knife, so their scandal would be a 'tail-gate'.
explanation.definitionFit: Driving inches behind another car is a straightforward verb sense of closely pursuing.

clue.text: Lunchtime snack to get on publicity platform

parts.note: a sandwich is a typical light midday bite
to board a bus or train is to get on it

explanation.surface: Someone grabs a lunchtime snack before mounting a stage for publicity.
explanation.definitionFit: A pair of hinged advertising placards worn by a person walking the street serves as a platform for publicity.

clue.text: The law, strangely, that can make you rich

indicators.note: the words are arranged strangely, i.e. their letters are put in an odd new order

explanation.surface: A cynical remark that the law, oddly enough, can make you rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strangely' scrambles the six letters of THE LAW.
explanation.definitionFit: Riches and affluence are what a fortune in money or property amounts to.

clue.text: Negligent on subject of young girl?

parts.note: re means concerning or on the subject of, as in letter headings
a miss is a young unmarried woman or girl

explanation.surface: Someone is accused of carelessness regarding a young girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Careless or lax in one's duty is the usual sense, a close synonym of negligent.

clue.text: More to benefit after reforms: none too soon!

indicators.note: the words come out once reformed, i.e. reshaped into a fresh order

explanation.surface: A political complaint that benefits only improved after reforms, and late at that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after reforms' rearranges the thirteen letters of MORE TO BENEFIT.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom meaning something happened at last, when it was overdue, the same as saying none too soon.

clue.text: Posh car seen in commercial

indicators.note: the letters are visible inside the single word that follows

explanation.surface: A luxury car appears in a television advertisement.
explanation.definitionFit: Short informal name for a Mercedes-Benz, a classic upmarket German motor.

clue.text: Artist seized by girl in combat

indicators.note: the artist is held or grabbed inside the girl's name

parts.note: Kate is a girl's name
RA is a Royal Academician, the usual crossword artist

explanation.surface: A painter is grabbed by a girl during a fight.
explanation.definitionFit: A Japanese unarmed fighting discipline using strikes and kicks, a form of combat.

clue.text: Some sent back Melchizedek, overenthusiastically summoned

indicators.note: sent back says the hidden letters are read backwards
Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some people rejected the biblical priest-king Melchizedek, having summoned him too eagerly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' picks DEKOVE out of 'Melchizedek, overenthusiastically'; 'sent back' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: To call up a memory or spirit is to conjure or call it forth, a synonym of summoned.

clue.text: Cold, boy dressed

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A shivering boy has got his clothes on.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothed or attired is the literary sense, meaning wearing garments.

clue.text: ABC a kid learned initially, awfully relaxed

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the following word is used
the letters are put together awfully, i.e. in a jumbled mess

explanation.surface: A kid learning the alphabet did so terribly, though in a carefree way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes L from 'learned'; 'awfully' scrambles ABCAKID with that L.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy-going and unhurried is the informal sense, a synonym of relaxed.

clue.text: Lots of churchgoers: capital fellows!

parts.note: Paris is the capital of France
hes are males, men or fellows

explanation.surface: An exclamation about crowds of worshippers in a capital full of men.
explanation.definitionFit: Local church congregations or communities, each one served by its own church and clergy.

clue.text: Close finishes in the Medallion Shield

indicators.note: the final letters of each of the following words are taken

explanation.surface: A tight contest decides the Medallion Shield, a sporting trophy.
explanation.definitionFit: The conclusion or finish of something, as in the close of play.

clue.text: Account in Financial Times is the truth

indicators.note: the account abbreviation goes in between the newspaper's two letters

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times newspaper

explanation.surface: A report in the business paper is presented as gospel.
explanation.definitionFit: Something actually true and verifiable, as opposed to fiction or opinion.

clue.text: Tories with less than intelligent contract

parts.note: Con is the abbreviation for Conservative, the party of the Tories
dense means stupid, not bright

explanation.surface: A jibe that Conservative politicians are rather dim, with a contract involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contract' looks like a noun in a political surface; it is the verb, to compress.
explanation.definitionFit: To shorten or compress into fewer words or less space, a verb sense of contract.

clue.text: Girl having wager with husband

parts.note: a bet is a wager
H is the abbreviation for husband in genealogy

explanation.surface: A woman places a bet together with her husband.
explanation.definitionFit: A short form of Elizabeth used as a female first name.

clue.text: Appreciating commercial, note piece of jewellery

parts.note: an ad is a commercial
mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale
a ring is worn on a finger

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys an advertisement featuring a note and a ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Regarding with pleasure or respect, a participle synonym of appreciating.

clue.text: Rare creature? Yes, you can say that again!

indicators.note: the phrase invites saying the word for yes a second time

parts.note: aye is an old or nautical word for yes

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic agreement about some unusual animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'you can say that again' is a common phrase of strong agreement, here also asking for AYE twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A Madagascan lemur, endangered and seldom seen, so a scarce animal.

clue.text: When do many set out for work?

definitions.text: When do many set out for work?

indicators.note: the letters are laid out afresh, in a different order

explanation.surface: A question about which day most people head off to their jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set out' rearranges DO MANY; the whole clue is also the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The first weekday, when the working week starts and commuters return to their jobs.

clue.text: Early 17th century banjo ace played

indicators.note: the letters are played around with, i.e. rearranged

explanation.surface: An ace banjo player performing music from the early 1600s.
explanation.definitionFit: Of the reign of James I of England, 1603 to 1625, whose Latin name is Jacobus.

clue.text: Neighbour having an objection

parts.note: a but is an objection, as in no ifs or buts

explanation.surface: A neighbour who keeps raising objections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neighbour' looks like a noun but is the verb, to border on.
explanation.definitionFit: To border or adjoin something is to neighbour it, used as a verb.

clue.text: Something in the Cherry Orchard: Turgenev, oddly

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters, first, third, fifth and seventh, are taken

explanation.surface: A literary aside on The Cherry Orchard, wrongly crediting Turgenev rather than Chekhov.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' hints the play's author is wrong (it is Chekhov's) while taking alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherry orchard is full of fruit-bearing woody plants, each one an example.

clue.text: One hunted for somewhere to get stone

definitions.meaning: the animal pursued by a hunter, its prey
an open pit from which stone is dug or blasted

explanation.surface: Someone on the run seeks out a source of stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: the prey a hunter chases, and an excavation where building stone is extracted.

clue.text: Not far from St Malo resort

indicators.note: read as re-sort, the letters are sorted again into a new order

explanation.surface: A holiday spot close to the French resort of St Malo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' poses as a seaside town; read it as re-sort, scrambling ST MALO.
explanation.definitionFit: Nearly or very nearly, as in almost there, meaning not far from it.
